questions.q: What is the three-call pattern used in essentially every PyTorch training loop with an optimizer?
options: model.train(), model.eval(), model.save()
optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward(), optimizer.step()
optimizer.step(), loss.backward(), optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward(), optimizer.zero_grad(), model.forward()
questions.explain: The standard order is: clear old gradients with zero_grad(), compute new gradients with backward(), then apply the update with step(). This ordering matters -- zero_grad() must come before backward() accumulates new gradients, and step() must come after.

options: It computes the loss for the current batch
It reads the .grad attribute of every parameter the optimizer was given and applies that optimizer's specific update rule to each one
It resets all gradients to zero
It moves the model to a different device
questions.explain: optimizer.step() is where the actual parameter update happens, using whatever gradients are currently stored in each tracked parameter's .grad, combined with the optimizer's own update rule (plain subtraction for SGD, momentum-adjusted for SGD with momentum, adaptive for Adam).

questions.q: What does adding momentum (e.g. optim.SGD(params, lr=0.01, momentum=0.9)) change about the update?
options: It ignores the current gradient entirely and uses only past gradients
It uses a running average of recent gradients, rather than just the current one, to smooth the update and reduce oscillation in narrow loss landscapes
It doubles the learning rate automatically
It disables gradient tracking for faster computation
questions.explain: Momentum maintains a running average (exponentially weighted by the momentum coefficient) of past gradients and uses that smoothed direction for the update, which helps dampen oscillation and can accelerate convergence in consistent directions.

questions.q: What does Adam add on top of what momentum alone provides?
options: Nothing; Adam and SGD with momentum are mathematically identical
A per-parameter adaptive learning rate, derived from a running average of squared gradients, which automatically shrinks the step for parameters receiving large or noisy gradients
The ability to train without a loss function
Automatic batch size tuning
questions.explain: Adam tracks two running averages: one of gradients (like momentum) and one of squared gradients, using the second to scale each parameter's effective learning rate individually -- making it more forgiving of an imperfect global learning rate choice.

questions.q: Why does optim.Adam typically use a much smaller default learning rate (0.001) than optim.SGD (often 0.01-0.1)?
options: Adam's learning rate has no real effect on training
Adam's adaptive per-parameter scaling already adjusts the effective step size based on gradient history, so a smaller base learning rate is appropriate and typical
It is an arbitrary convention with no underlying reason
Smaller learning rates are required for GPU training but not CPU
questions.explain: Because Adam already adapts the effective step size per parameter using its running statistics, a smaller nominal learning rate tends to work well, whereas plain SGD relies entirely on the chosen lr and benefits from a larger value.
